growth_story.headline: After the 1994 genocide, Rwanda grew fast for almost three decades on aid and public building; now debt is rising and good jobs lag.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person shrank by 0.4 percent a year on average: falling coffee, tea and mineral prices had already weakened the economy, civil war began in 1990, and the 1994 genocide cut income per person by 41.5 percent in one year before a 61.9 percent rebound in 1995. From 1998 to 2025 growth averaged 5.0 percent a year, as the state led the rebuilding through large public projects paid for mostly by foreign aid. The pace eased a little, from 5.1 percent a year in 2006 to 2015 to 4.5 percent in 2016 to 2025, and the IMF says growth slowed in the 2010s as productivity gains faded and public investment took the place of private activity. Covid brought the one sharp fall of this later era, 4.9 percent in 2020, but growth came back quickly and reached 7.0 percent in 2025. Income per person stood at its highest level yet in 2025, while the IMF and World Bank describe growth still carried by construction and public investment, with big projects such as a new airport paid for more and more with debt.

threads.title: Collapse and genocide in the 1990s
threads.text: Falling world prices for coffee, tea and minerals had already slowed the economy before civil war began in 1990. The 1994 genocide destroyed lives, institutions and trade links, and income per person fell by 41.5 percent that year.

citations.title: Rwanda Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: But as world market prices fell for minerals, coffee, and tea, and fiscal difficulties increased, the economy began to falter.

citations.title: Rwanda Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: Within a year the country’s GDP fell, from an already low base, by half and Rwanda became the second poorest country in the world

citations.title: Rwanda Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: The social and physical infrastructure was devastated, trade links were ruptured, businesses and agricultural assets dwindled, and institutions of governance required rebuilding.

threads.title: Aid-financed rebuilding led by the state
threads.text: With almost no private sector left, the state led the recovery through large public projects, mostly paid for by foreign aid. For the 2000s the IMF also credits productivity gains and private investment drawn in by foreign firms and privatization, especially in phones and internet.

citations.title: Rwanda Systematic Country Diagnostic
citations.quote: In the absence of a viable private sector, the state led the economic recovery efforts through large public investments, mostly financed through external assistance.

citations.title: Rwanda: 2025 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review Under the Policy Coordination Instrument—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: Growth was driven by productivity gains and private investment spurred by FDI and privatization, particularly in ICT

threads.title: Public building, fading private investment
threads.text: From the 2010s the IMF describes public investment taking the place of private activity, above all in construction, as productivity gains faded. It finds that the share of growth coming from private investment kept falling through 2024.

citations.title: Rwanda: 2025 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review Under the Policy Coordination Instrument—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: Growth eased as productivity gains waned, public investment increasingly substituted for private activity, particularly in the construction sector.

citations.title: Rwanda: 2025 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review Under the Policy Coordination Instrument—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: construction-driven public investments, although the contribution of private investment continued to decline

threads.title: Shocks, an airport and debt
threads.text: Covid, floods in 2023 and a Marburg disease outbreak in 2024 came in quick succession. Public debt is high, and the IMF expects borrowing for the New Kigali International Airport to push it higher.

citations.title: Rwanda: 2025 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review Under the Policy Coordination Instrument—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: including navigating the post-COVID-19 pandemic era, the 2023 floods, the 2024 Marburg disease outbreak, and other global disruptions

citations.title: Rwanda: 2025 Article IV Consultation and Sixth Review Under the Policy Coordination Instrument—Press Release; and Staff Report
citations.quote: Nevertheless, borrowing for the NKIA project is expected to push public debt near 80 percent of GDP by 2027.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: Public debt remains elevated, at about 73 percent in 2025

threads.title: Jobs that lag growth
threads.text: The World Bank finds that job creation has broadly kept pace with the growing working-age population. But most new jobs are informal, short-term and low-paid, and young people, women and rural workers fare worst.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: broadly keeping pace with growth in the working-age population, most new jobs are informal, temporary, and low-paid

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: with youth, women, and rural workers facing particularly weak labor-market outcomes

since_last_year.text: Growth sped up again: income per person rose 7.0 percent in 2025 in the data, and the World Bank reports broad growth into early 2026, led by industry, services and a recovery in farming. Prices then rose faster in the first half of 2026, partly because of the conflict in the Middle East, and the central bank raised its policy rate.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: Growth was broad-based, led by industry, services, and a recovery in agriculture.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: Inflation pressures partly driven by the conflict in Middle East had built up in the first half of 2026

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Rwanda
citations.quote: In response, the central bank raised the policy rate by a cumulative 200 bps, bringing it to 8.75 percent in August 2026.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says demand and supply shocks caused a recession in 2016 to 2018, but in the data income per person kept growing in each of those years: 3.2 percent in 2016, 2.3 in 2017 and 5.6 in 2018. The World Bank's figure for average growth in income per person over 2016 to 2025 is also slightly higher than the data's 4.5.
